# Why discrete time

## The world arrives in steps

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="36%"}
- Case counts come daily or weekly
- Computers advance in fixed steps
- Most forecasting models step by day
- The ODE is the smooth curve underneath
:::
::: {.column width="64%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
base = ({N: 1000, S0: 990, I0: 10, beta: 0.05, c: 10, gamma: 0.25, tmax: 40})
colS = "#4682b4"
colI = "#b22222"
colR = "#2e8b57"
rateToProb = (r, dt) => 1 - Math.exp(-r * dt)
mapStep = (u, p, dt) => {
  const [S, I, R] = u
  const inf = rateToProb(p.beta * p.c * I / p.N, dt) * S
  const rec = rateToProb(p.gamma, dt) * I
  return [S - inf, I + inf - rec, R + rec]
}
mulberry32 = (seed) => {
  let a = seed >>> 0
  return () => {
    a = (a + 0x6D2B79F5) | 0
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a)
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296
  }
}
binomial = (n, p, rng) => {
  let k = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (rng() < p) k++
  return k
}
chainStep = (u, p, dt, rng) => {
  const [S, I, R] = u
  const Y = binomial(S, rateToProb(p.beta * p.c * I / p.N, dt), rng)
  const Z = binomial(I, rateToProb(p.gamma, dt), rng)
  return [S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z]
}
iterate = (stepFn, p, dt, nsteps) => {
  let u = [p.S0, p.I0, 0]
  const out = [{t: 0, S: u[0], I: u[1], R: u[2]}]
  for (let k = 1; k <= nsteps; k++) {
    u = stepFn(u, p, dt)
    out.push({t: k * dt, S: u[0], I: u[1], R: u[2]})
  }
  return out
}
sirRhs = (u, p) => {
  const lam = p.beta * p.c * u[1] / p.N
  return [-lam * u[0], lam * u[0] - p.gamma * u[1], p.gamma * u[1]]
}
rk4 = (p, h, tmax) => {
  let u = [p.S0, p.I0, 0]
  const n = Math.round(tmax / h)
  const out = [{t: 0, S: u[0], I: u[1], R: u[2]}]
  for (let k = 1; k <= n; k++) {
    const k1 = sirRhs(u, p)
    const k2 = sirRhs(u.map((x, i) => x + h / 2 * k1[i]), p)
    const k3 = sirRhs(u.map((x, i) => x + h / 2 * k2[i]), p)
    const k4 = sirRhs(u.map((x, i) => x + h * k3[i]), p)
    u = u.map((x, i) => x + h / 6 * (k1[i] + 2 * k2[i] + 2 * k3[i] + k4[i]))
    out.push({t: k * h, S: u[0], I: u[1], R: u[2]})
  }
  return out
}
ode = rk4(base, 0.01, base.tmax)
odeCurve = ode.filter((d, i) => i % 10 === 0)
odeEnd = ode[ode.length - 1]
mapBase = iterate(mapStep, base, 1, 40)
longRows = (rows, which) => rows.flatMap((d) => [
  {t: d.t, value: d.S, comp: "S", which},
  {t: d.t, value: d.I, comp: "I", which},
  {t: d.t, value: d.R, comp: "R", which}
])
dailyCases = Array.from({length: 40}, (_, k) => ({
  day: k + 1, cases: ode[k * 100].S - ode[(k + 1) * 100].S
}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 580, marginLeft: 90, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {label: "day", domain: [0, 41], ticks: [0, 10, 20, 30, 40],
    labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "new cases reported that day (people)", ticks: 5,
    labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(dailyCases, {x1: (d) => d.day - 0.45, x2: (d) => d.day + 0.45,
      y: "cases", fill: colS}),
    Plot.line(odeCurve, {x: (d) => d.t + 0.5,
      y: (d) => base.beta * base.c * d.I * d.S / base.N, stroke: "#17242b",
      strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```
::: {.attribution}
Bars: daily counts from the baseline SIR scenario, N = 1000, R~0~ = 2. Line: the ODE's rate of new infections.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Data come in bins.
Simulations step.
So it is natural to write the model in steps too.
Today we ask what stepping does to the ODE we met this morning, and what changes once we let whole people move at random.
:::

::: {.aside}
Stepping is older than the epidemic models. The chain binomial gave epidemics their first stochastic form.
:::

::: {.notes}
Euler wrote the step rule in 1768.
Reed and Frost taught the chain binomial at Johns Hopkins in 1928 but never published it. Helen Abbey wrote it up in 1952.
Greenwood's 1931 version has a fixed risk per step, whatever the number infectious.
Bailey's 1957 book gathered the stochastic theory in one place.
:::

# The map approximates the ODE

## Why a rate becomes a probability

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- The ODE moves people at rate $r$ per day
- Slice the step into $n$ slivers
- In one sliver the chance is $r\,\delta t / n$
- Survive all $n$, then let $n \to \infty$

$$
\Bigl(1 - \frac{r\,\delta t}{n}\Bigr)^{n} \longrightarrow e^{-r\,\delta t}
$$

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
nSliver = {
  while (true) {
    for (const n of [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64]) {
      yield n
      await Promises.delay(n === 64 ? 2500 : 1300)
    }
  }
}
md`At r δt = 1: (1 − 1/${nSliver})<sup>${nSliver}</sup> = **${Math.pow(1 - 1 / nSliver, nSliver).toFixed(3)}**, and e<sup>−1</sup> = ${Math.exp(-1).toFixed(3)}`
```
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sliverRows = Array.from({length: 121}, (_, i) => i * 0.025).flatMap((x) => [
  {x, y: Math.pow(Math.max(0, 1 - x / nSliver), nSliver),
    which: `${nSliver} sliver${nSliver > 1 ? "s" : ""}`},
  {x, y: Math.exp(-x), which: "exp(−r δt)"}
])
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 90, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  title: `${nSliver} sliver${nSliver > 1 ? "s" : ""}: the chance of surviving the whole step`,
  x: {label: "r δt (rate × step, dimensionless)", domain: [0, 3],
    labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "chance of no event in the step", domain: [0, 1],
    ticks: [0, 0.5, 1], labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  color: {domain: [`${nSliver} sliver${nSliver > 1 ? "s" : ""}`, "exp(−r δt)"],
    range: ["#17242b", colI], legend: true,
    swatchSize: 22, style: {fontSize: "22px"}},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(sliverRows, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleX([1], {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
    Plot.dot([{x: 1, y: Math.pow(1 - 1 / nSliver, nSliver)}],
      {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "#17242b", r: 9}),
    Plot.dot([{x: 1, y: Math.exp(-1)}], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: colI, r: 9})
  ]
})
```
::: {.attribution}
The slivers multiply. More slivers, and the product settles on the exponential.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The ODE speaks in rates. A rate is a chance per tiny sliver of time.
Cut the step into n slivers. Each is survived with chance one minus r delta t over n. Survive the step means survive every sliver, so multiply.
Let the slivers shrink. The product tends to the exponential. That is the definition of e, the same limit as compound interest.
So a constant rate over a step gives an exponential survival, and the rest follows.
:::

## From a rate to a probability

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Chance of no event in $\delta t$: $e^{-r\delta t}$
- So $p = 1 - e^{-r\delta t}$
- $r\delta t$ is the expected number of events, not a chance
- It can exceed one. $p$ cannot

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rdt = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "r δt"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`r δt = ${rdt.toFixed(2)} gives p = ${(1 - Math.exp(-rdt)).toFixed(3)}`
```
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rateRows = Array.from({length: 121}, (_, i) => i * 0.025).flatMap((x) => [
  {x, y: 1 - Math.exp(-x), which: "p = 1 − exp(−r δt)"},
  {x, y: x, which: "r δt"}
])
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 90, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {label: "r δt (rate × step, dimensionless)", domain: [0, 3],
    labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "probability in one step", domain: [0, 1.5],
    ticks: [0, 0.5, 1, 1.5], labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  color: {domain: ["p = 1 − exp(−r δt)", "r δt"], range: [colI, "#888"],
    legend: true,
    swatchSize: 22, style: {fontSize: "22px"}},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: "#17242b", strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 2.95, y: 1.06, label: "p cannot exceed 1"}],
      {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", textAnchor: "end", fill: "#17242b"}),
    Plot.line(rateRows, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleX([rdt], {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
    Plot.dot([{x: rdt, y: 1 - Math.exp(-rdt)}], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: colI,
      r: 9}),
    Plot.dot([{x: rdt, y: rdt}], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "#888", r: 9})
  ]
})
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
One minus the survival chance is the chance the event happens at least once.
r delta t is the expected number of events in the step. For a small step that is nearly the same as the probability, so the two lines agree at the left.
For a large step the expected count goes past one, but a person can only leave once. The exponential form keeps p between zero and one.
:::

## The deterministic map

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Per person, per step

::: {.bigmath}
$$
p_I = 1 - e^{-\beta c I_t \delta t / N}, \qquad
p_R = 1 - e^{-\gamma \delta t}
$$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
Move the expected numbers

::: {.bigmath}
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{t+1} &= S_t - p_I S_t \\
I_{t+1} &= I_t + p_I S_t - p_R I_t \\
R_{t+1} &= R_t + p_R I_t
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::
::::

::: {.aside}
Same ingredients as the ODE: force of infection $\lambda = \beta c I / N$ and recovery rate $\gamma$. The state stays continuous.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two probabilities from two rates.
Then move the expected number of people in each flow.
Sum the three lines: the population is conserved.
The counts have decimals. The map moves fractions of people.
Nothing is random yet.
:::

## What a time step is

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Take the state at day $t$
- Move people once, all together
- Land at day $t + \delta t$
- Repeat

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tick = {
  while (true) {
    for (let k = 0; k <= 40; k++) {
      yield k
      await Promises.delay(k === 40 ? 2500 : 180)
    }
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tickState = mapBase[tick]
md`Day ${tick}: S = ${tickState.S.toFixed(1)}, I = ${tickState.I.toFixed(1)}, R = ${tickState.R.toFixed(1)}`
```
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tickRows = longRows(mapBase.slice(0, tick + 1), "map")
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 90, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {label: "time (days)", domain: [0, 40], labelAnchor: "center",
    labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "people", domain: [0, 1000], ticks: [0, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000],
    labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  color: {domain: ["S", "I", "R"], range: [colS, colI, colR], legend: true,
    swatchSize: 22, style: {fontSize: "22px"}},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(longRows(odeCurve, "ode"), {x: "t", y: "value", stroke: "comp",
      strokeWidth: 2, strokeOpacity: 0.3}),
    ...(tick > 0 ? [Plot.line(tickRows, {x: "t", y: "value", stroke: "comp",
      strokeWidth: 3})] : []),
    Plot.dot(tickRows, {x: "t", y: "value", fill: "comp", r: 6}),
    Plot.ruleX([tick], {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "6,4"})
  ]
})
```
::: {.attribution}
Dots: the map, one step per day, playing on a loop. Faint lines: the ODE.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Watch it tick.
Each step takes the whole population from one day to the next in one go.
Notice the dots do not sit exactly on the faint ODE curve. That is the next slide.
:::

## Shrink the step

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Compare the map with the ODE
- Large steps overshoot the peak
- Small steps sit on the curve

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
dtChoice = {
  while (true) {
    for (const dt of [4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1]) {
      yield dt
      await Promises.delay(dt === 0.1 ? 2500 : 1500)
    }
  }
}
mapDt = iterate(mapStep, base, dtChoice, Math.round(40 / dtChoice))
md`δt = **${dtChoice}** ${dtChoice === 1 ? "day" : "days"}<br>
Peak I: map **${Math.max(...mapDt.map((d) => d.I)).toFixed(0)}**, ODE ${Math.max(...ode.map((d) => d.I)).toFixed(0)}`
```
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 90, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {label: "time (days)", domain: [0, 40], labelAnchor: "center",
    labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "infectious I (people)", domain: [0, 320],
    ticks: [0, 100, 200, 300], labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  color: {domain: ["ODE", "map"], range: [colI, "#17242b"], legend: true,
    swatchSize: 22, style: {fontSize: "22px"}},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(odeCurve.map((d) => ({...d, which: "ODE"})),
      {x: "t", y: "I", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 4}),
    Plot.line(mapDt.map((d) => ({...d, which: "map"})),
      {x: "t", y: "I", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 3, strokeDasharray: "8,6"}),
    Plot.dot(mapDt, {x: "t", y: "I", fill: "#17242b", r: 4})
  ]
})
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
It cycles from four days down to a tenth of a day.
At four days the map is crude. By a tenth of a day the dashed line is on the ODE.
The map is a first-order method. It is Euler's step with the rate wrapped in an exponential.
:::

## Halve the step, halve the error

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Error at day 40 against the ODE
- Log axes, slope one guide
- First order: error $\propto \delta t$
- The map converges to the ODE
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
dtList = [4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.03125, 0.015625]
errRows = dtList.map((dt) => {
  const traj = iterate(mapStep, base, dt, Math.round(40 / dt))
  const end = traj[traj.length - 1]
  const err = Math.max(Math.abs(end.S - odeEnd.S), Math.abs(end.I - odeEnd.I),
    Math.abs(end.R - odeEnd.R))
  return {dt, err}
})
guideRows = dtList.map((dt) => ({
  dt, err: errRows[errRows.length - 1].err * dt / dtList[dtList.length - 1]
}))
errShown = {
  while (true) {
    for (let k = 1; k <= dtList.length; k++) {
      yield k
      await Promises.delay(k === dtList.length ? 3000 : 600)
    }
  }
}
errNow = errRows[errShown - 1]
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 100, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {type: "log", label: "step δt (days)", labelAnchor: "center",
    labelOffset: 55, ticks: [0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 4],
    tickFormat: (d) => String(d)},
  y: {type: "log", label: "max |map − ODE| at day 40 (people)",
    labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40,
    ticks: [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200], tickFormat: (d) => String(d)},
  color: {domain: ["measured", "slope 1"], range: [colS, "#17242b"],
    legend: true,
    swatchSize: 22, style: {fontSize: "22px"}},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(guideRows.map((d) => ({...d, which: "slope 1"})),
      {x: "dt", y: "err", stroke: "which", strokeDasharray: "8,6",
       strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(errRows.slice(0, errShown).map((d) => ({...d, which: "measured"})),
      {x: "dt", y: "err", fill: "which", r: 8}),
    Plot.text([errNow], {x: "dt", y: "err",
      text: (d) => `${d.err.toFixed(1)} people`,
      dx: 16, dy: -18, textAnchor: "start", fill: colS})
  ]
})
```
::: {.attribution}
Largest absolute difference across S, I and R at day 40, computed live against a fine Runge-Kutta solution. The step halves each beat.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Both axes are logarithmic.
The points run parallel to the guide with slope one.
Halve the step and the error halves. That is what first order means.
This is the first limit: the map tends to the ODE.
:::

# The chain adds randomness

## Each person flips a coin

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- $S$ susceptibles, each infected with probability $p_I$
- Independent coins
- The count of heads is Binomial($S$, $p_I$)
- Whole people, and a different answer each draw

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pFlip = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.5], {value: 0.2, step: 0.01,
  label: htl.html`p<sub>I</sub>`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
coinAnim = {
  let seed = 0
  while (true) {
    seed += 1
    const rng = mulberry32(100 + seed)
    yield Array.from({length: 100}, () => rng() < pFlip)
    await Promises.delay(1500)
  }
}
flips = coinAnim.map((hit, i) => ({
  x: i % 10, y: Math.floor(i / 10), state: hit ? "I" : "S"
}))
md`Infected: **${flips.filter((d) => d.state === "I").length}** of 100.
Expected: **${(100 * pFlip).toFixed(0)}**`
```
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 600, inset: 30, style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {axis: null}, y: {axis: null},
  color: {domain: ["S", "I"], range: [colS, colI]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(flips, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "state", r: 22})
  ]
})
```
::: {.attribution}
100 susceptibles. A fresh set of coins every 1.5 seconds.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Same probability as before. Now each susceptible flips a coin.
Watch the count. Each redraw lands somewhere around the expected value.
That count is a binomial draw. This is the whole difference between the map and the chain.
:::

## The stochastic chain

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Draw the numbers who move

::: {.bigmath}
$$
Y_t \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(S_t, p_I)
$$
$$
Z_t \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(I_t, p_R)
$$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
Then update the counts

::: {.bigmath}
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{t+1} &= S_t - Y_t \\
I_{t+1} &= I_t + Y_t - Z_t \\
R_{t+1} &= R_t + Z_t
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::
::::

::: {.aside}
Given the state at $t$, the map moves exactly what the chain expects: $\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = p_I S_t$ and $\mathbb{E}[Z_t] = p_R I_t$. The state is now integer.
:::

::: {.notes}
Same two probabilities.
Replace the expected numbers with binomial draws.
The map is the one-step expectation of the chain. That is the link. It is also where the link ends.
:::

## Three models, one set of rates {.tight-code}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
ODE

```julia
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    return nothing
end
```

- Rates in, derivatives out
- A solver chooses the steps
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
Map and chain

```julia
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

function sir_map_step(state, p, δt)          # deterministic, eq-ch02-map
    S, I, R = state
    infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    recovery  = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    return (S - infection, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery)
end

function sir_chain_step(state, p, δt, rng)   # stochastic, eq-ch02-chain
    S, I, R = state
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt)))
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt)))
    return (S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z)
end
```
:::
::::

::: {.attribution}
The kernels from the chapters, unchanged. `-expm1(-x)` is `1 - exp(-x)` computed accurately for small `x`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Same rates in all three.
The ODE hands them to a solver.
The map converts them to probabilities and multiplies.
The chain converts them to probabilities and draws. Two lines differ.
:::

## Reed and Frost, 1928

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Reed-Frost

::: {.bigmath}
$$
S_{t+1} = S_t\,(1 - p)^{I_t}
$$
:::

::: {.sub}
Expected survivors, each infectious contact infects with probability $p$.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Our chain

::: {.bigmath}
$$
\mathbb{E}[S_{t+1}] = S_t\,e^{-\beta c I_t \delta t / N}
$$
:::

::: {.sub}
The same, with the per-step infection probability $p_I = 1 - e^{-\beta c I_t \delta t / N}$.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.big}
$(1 - p)^{I} \approx e^{-pI}$ for small $p$, so with $p = \beta c\,\delta t / N$ they agree
:::

::: {.notes}
Reed and Frost wrote the escape probability as a product over infectious contacts.
We wrote it as an exponential of the total hazard.
For small per-contact probability the two are the same chain.
:::

## Many runs

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Grey: single runs of the chain
- Red: their mean
- Black dashed: the map
- Runs pile up into a fan

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof seedChoice = Inputs.range([1, 50], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "seed"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ensAnim = {
  while (true) {
    const runs = []
    for (let j = 0; j < 100; j++) {
      const rng = mulberry32(seedChoice * 1000 + j)
      runs.push(iterate((u, p, dt) => chainStep(u, p, dt, rng), base, 1, 40))
      yield runs.slice()
      await Promises.delay(80)
    }
    await Promises.delay(3000)
  }
}
ensemble = ensAnim
extinct = ensemble.filter((traj) => traj[40].I === 0).length
md`Extinct by day 40: **${extinct} of ${ensemble.length}** runs
(${(100 * extinct / ensemble.length).toFixed(0)}%)`
```
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ensRows = ensemble.flatMap((traj, j) => traj.map((d) => ({
  t: d.t, I: d.I, run: j, which: "chain runs"
})))
ensMean = Array.from({length: 41}, (_, k) => ({
  t: k, I: d3.mean(ensemble, (traj) => traj[k].I), which: "chain mean"
}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 90, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {label: "time (days)", domain: [0, 40], labelAnchor: "center",
    labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "infectious I (people)", domain: [0, 320],
    ticks: [0, 100, 200, 300], labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  color: {domain: ["chain runs", "chain mean", "map"],
    range: ["#999", colI, "#17242b"], legend: true,
    swatchSize: 22, style: {fontSize: "22px"}},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(ensRows, {x: "t", y: "I", z: "run", stroke: "which",
      strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
    ...(ensemble.length >= 10 ? [
      Plot.line(ensMean, {x: "t", y: "I", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 4}),
      Plot.line(mapBase.map((d) => ({...d, which: "map"})),
        {x: "t", y: "I", stroke: "which", strokeWidth: 3,
         strokeDasharray: "8,6"})
    ] : [])
  ]
})
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
One run is one possible epidemic.
Runs pile up to a hundred. Once ten are in, the mean appears and settles. The map runs close to it but peaks higher.
Some runs never take off. The map cannot do that.
It loops. The seed slider gives a different set of runs if you want one.
:::

## The map is not the mean of the chain

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- New infections per step bend over as $I$ grows
- The map steps from the average $I$
- The chain steps each run, then averages: lower
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fInf = (I) => base.S0 * rateToProb(base.beta * base.c * I / base.N, 2)
jCurve = Array.from({length: 101}, (_, i) => ({I: i * 10, f: fInf(i * 10)}))
jA = 100
jB = 900
jMid = (jA + jB) / 2
jMeanF = (fInf(jA) + fInf(jB)) / 2
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 100, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  marginRight: 50, style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {label: "infectious now, I (people)", domain: [0, 1000],
    labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "new infections in one step (people)", domain: [0, 700],
    ticks: [0, 200, 400, 600], labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(jCurve, {x: "I", y: "f", stroke: "#17242b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line([{I: jA, f: fInf(jA)}, {I: jB, f: fInf(jB)}],
      {x: "I", y: "f", stroke: "#999", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "8,6"}),
    Plot.ruleX([jMid], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.dot([{I: jA, f: fInf(jA)}, {I: jB, f: fInf(jB)}],
      {x: "I", y: "f", fill: "#999", r: 8}),
    Plot.dot([{I: jMid, f: fInf(jMid)}], {x: "I", y: "f", fill: colI, r: 10}),
    Plot.dot([{I: jMid, f: jMeanF}], {x: "I", y: "f", fill: "#555", r: 10}),
    Plot.text([{I: jMid, f: fInf(jMid), label: "map: f(mean of I)"}],
      {x: "I", y: "f", text: "label", dx: 14, dy: -22, textAnchor: "start",
       fill: colI}),
    Plot.text([{I: jMid, f: jMeanF, label: "chain: mean of f(I)"}],
      {x: "I", y: "f", text: "label", dx: 14, dy: 26, textAnchor: "start",
       fill: "#555"}),
    Plot.text([{I: jA, f: fInf(jA), label: "run A"}, {I: jB, f: fInf(jB),
      label: "run B"}], {x: "I", y: "f", text: "label", dy: 30, fill: "#555"})
  ]
})
```
::: {.attribution}
Two runs, A and B, with the same S. Drawn with δt = 2 days so the gap is visible.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Take two runs with different numbers infectious.
The map steps from their average. The chain steps each and then averages.
The curve bends, so the two answers differ. Jensen's inequality.
Peaks that land on different days flatten the mean further.
:::

## Bigger populations, smaller wobbles

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Same initial fraction, $I_0 = N / 100$
- Spread in $I/N$ shrinks like $1 / \sqrt{N}$
- Small $N$: extinction is common
- Large $N$: runs look like the ODE

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof Nchoice = Inputs.radio([100, 1000, 10000], {value: 1000, label: "N"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
nEns = {
  const p = {...base, N: Nchoice, S0: Nchoice - Nchoice / 100,
    I0: Nchoice / 100}
  return Array.from({length: 100}, (_, j) => {
    const rng = mulberry32(7 + j)
    return iterate((u, pp, dt) => chainStep(u, pp, dt, rng), p, 1, 40)
  })
}
nSpread = d3.max(d3.range(41), (k) => d3.deviation(nEns,
  (traj) => traj[k].I / Nchoice))
md`Largest run-to-run sd of I/N: **${nSpread.toFixed(3)}**.
Extinct: **${nEns.filter((traj) => traj[40].I === 0).length}** of 100`
```
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
nRows = nEns.flatMap((traj, j) => traj.map((d) => ({
  t: d.t, frac: d.I / Nchoice, run: j
})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 1050, height: 600, marginLeft: 100, marginBottom: 70, marginTop: 30,
  style: {fontSize: "24px"},
  x: {label: "time (days)", domain: [0, 40], labelAnchor: "center",
    labelOffset: 55},
  y: {label: "infectious fraction I/N", domain: [0, 0.35],
    ticks: [0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3], labelAnchor: "top", labelOffset: 40},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(nRows, {x: "t", y: "frac", z: "run", stroke: "#999",
      strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
    Plot.line(odeCurve, {x: "t", y: (d) => d.I / base.N, stroke: colI,
      strokeWidth: 4})
  ]
})
```
::: {.attribution}
100 runs of the chain, δt = 1 day, at each N. Red: the ODE.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Demographic stochasticity: chance from moving whole people.
At a hundred people the fan is wide and many runs die out.
At ten thousand the runs hug the ODE.
Tenfold more people, the spread as a fraction falls to about a third.
:::

## One step, one move

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Both draws use the state at $t$
- Nobody is infected and recovers in the same step
- An artefact of the step, not of the disease
- It fades as $\delta t \to 0$
:::

Infections and recoveries are drawn side by side from the same starting state.
So a person infected in this step cannot also recover in it.
With a step of a day and a four-day infectious period this barely matters.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- A rate becomes a probability per step
- SEIR: a latent stage $E$
- SIRS: immunity wanes, $R \to S$
- Erlang stages: chain several $I$ boxes (Chapter 10)

## Summary

- The map is an Euler-like step. Shrink $\delta t$ and it becomes the ODE
- The chain moves whole people at random. Shrink $\delta t$ and it becomes a continuous-time Markov chain
- The map is the chain's one-step expectation, not its mean trajectory
- Randomness matters most when counts are small

::: {.notes}
Two discrete models, two different limits.
The map approximates the ODE. The chain approximates the continuous-time Markov chain, also called a jump process.
Keep both ideas apart and the rest of the course is easier.
:::
